newsitem.title: USA: Ford chief plays down impact of dlr-yen rise.
newsitem.headline: Ford chief plays down impact of dlr-yen rise.

text.p: Ford Motor Co President Jacques Nasser played down the negative effect of the rise in the dollar-yen exchange rate on competitiveness of U.S. exports.

In an exclusive interview with Reuters Financial Television (RFTV) on Tuesday, Nasser said, "Clearly the yen is a contributing factor to global competitiveness and 115 (yen per dollar) is not as good as 85 or 90, but it is one element only of our competitiveness equation."
Nasser said he avoids focusing on exchange rate as the only test of American or Japanese competitiveness because the situation is changing rather dramatically.
In explaining how the situation has changed, Nasser noted that the Japanese are sourcing more outside of Japan and American companies are sourcing more in other locations around the world.
"The footprint of exchange will vary from company to company," Nasser said.

The dollar sank to a post World War II low of 79.75 yen on April 19, 1995. Since then, the dollar has gained about 46 percent versus the Japanese currency, hitting a 45 month high of 117 yen earlier this week.
Nasser told RFTV that Ford Motor does not "bank" on any exchange rate.

"Exchange rates are really a fallout of economic conditions around the world and we're going to live with them. If it means trying harder and doing more in other areas of our cost elements, we'll just have to do it," he added.
Nasser emphasized that exchange rates are an element of strategy but do not drive strategy.
Last year, some leaders among U.S. automakers complained to the White House about the potential damage wrought by the dollar-yen rally.

When asked if he was planning to discuss with the Clinton Administration the current dollar-yen exchange rate and how it might affect competitiveness, Nasser replied, "No. At this point in my role at least, my focus is on getting the fundamentals of the business right."
"That really means looking at the cost elements (and) the investment elements of the business that we can influence," Nasser said.

When asked whether the Clinton Administration should have taken steps previously to stem the dollar's rise, Nasser responded: "I wouldn't want to offer advice in that area. I really want to look out to those areas of the business that I can influence."
